definition: The power to decide your own affairs without asking permission from a higher government.
The most important law of a country or state. All other laws must respect it.
When a region breaks away from a country to become independent.
Descendants of enslaved people who formed their own communities, called quilombos, and keep their lands and traditions.
To cancel a law or decision and remove its effect.
The highest court of a country. It rules on whether laws and government acts respect the constitution.
A vote in which the public directly approves or rejects a law.
Removing a politician from office before their term ends.
A rule that stops someone from holding the same office for more than a set number of terms.
Every adult can vote, with no exclusion by income, education, sex or race.
A government where power is concentrated in a few hands and there is little or no freedom to oppose it.
A government ban on being out in public during certain hours.
Helping a person with an incurable illness end their life, at their request, to avoid suffering.
Technology that identifies people by comparing a face filmed by a camera with photos stored in a database.
Organized crime groups that often control territory and illegal activities.
Romantic relationships with more than one person at the same time, with everyone's knowledge and consent.
A relationship in which the partners agree that each may have other partners.
Ways of speaking and writing that avoid marking masculine or feminine, such as "they" instead of "he or she".
How a person sees themself: a man, a woman, both or neither, regardless of the sex they were born with.
Acronym for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.
Setting aside a share of university places or jobs for people from certain racial groups.
A place where people of many cultures, languages and religions live together, each keeping their traditions.
Attacking an enemy first because you believe it is preparing to attack you.
An agreement between countries to reduce or eliminate certain kinds of weapons.
Weapons that pick and attack targets on their own, with a computer deciding instead of a person.
To convince someone not to attack by showing that the response would be severe.
Serious violations of the rules of war, such as attacking civilians or mistreating prisoners.
An organization that brings together nearly all countries to work on peace, human rights and cooperation.
Systematically killing or persecuting a people, ethnic group or religion with the intent to destroy it.
Troops sent abroad, under international coordination, to keep order in conflict zones.
Economic punishments against a country, such as blocking trade or freezing money abroad.
Agreements between countries to defend each other: if one is attacked, the others help.
Always following another country's or bloc's position instead of deciding case by case.
A formal agreement between countries, with rules both sides promise to follow.
Countries with very large military, economic or political power.
To take from those who have more and give to those who have less, through taxes, laws or public programs.
A sector or company essential for a country to function or defend itself, such as energy, oil, water or technology.
Companies controlled by the government.
Breaking up large rural estates to give land to people who want to farm it.
Workers' organizations that negotiate pay and working conditions on behalf of the group.
Money the state pays regularly to people in need, to guarantee a basic standard of living.
A Brazilian federal program that pays a monthly amount to low-income families.
A rule that makes it very hard to fire permanent government employees.
To support an activity with public money so it costs less or is more profitable.
The public institution that manages a country's currency and sets its basic interest rate.
The price of borrowed money. High rates make credit more expensive and tend to slow prices; low rates do the opposite.
A general, continuing rise in prices that makes money buy less. Its causes are debated: money creation, demand, costs.
The total taxes that people and companies pay, relative to the size of the economy.
The money the government collects from taxes.
A period when the economy shrinks: output falls and unemployment tends to rise.
The price of a country's currency compared with other currencies, such as the dollar.
Digital money, such as Bitcoin, that is not issued by any government or central bank.
A system in which the government decides what is produced, how much, and at what price.
A system in which prices and production come from free exchange between buyers and sellers, with little government interference.
Large domestic companies that the government chooses to back so they can grow and compete worldwide.
Government rules that set how an economic activity may operate.
A tax charged on imported goods that makes them more expensive.
Trade between countries with few or no tariffs or barriers.
A country's ability to make its own economic decisions without depending on other countries.
Companies that operate in several countries at once.
Bringing countries' economies closer through trade, investment and shared rules.
All the steps needed to make something, from raw materials to the finished product.
Crops whose genes were altered in a lab, for example to resist pests.
Chemicals used on crops to fight pests and plant diseases.
Altering the DNA of a living being to correct or change its traits.
The earliest stage of human development, in the first weeks after fertilization.
Devices placed in the brain to read its signals or stimulate mental activity.
Computer programs able to do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as understanding text or recognizing images.
Using machines and software to do work that people used to do.
Meat made in a lab from animal cells, without raising or slaughtering a whole animal.
Secretly obtaining information from another country, company or person.
The collection of weapons a country holds.
What a government considers good for the country as a whole, such as security, economy and influence in the world.
Institutions formed by several countries to handle shared issues, such as the UN or the WTO.
A person who feels part of all humanity before feeling part of a nation.
The elected body that makes a country's laws.
When different parties take turns governing as elections pass.
An open meeting where people decide together instead of electing representatives.
To make an act a crime, with a punishment set by law.
To make something allowed by law that used to be forbidden.
Transforming an economy to produce more in factories and with machines.
Extracting minerals from the ground, such as gold, iron and niobium.
Raising animals such as cattle for meat, milk and other products.
